title: Covalent structures and intermolecular forces
summary: Covalent substances are either giant networks or simple molecules. Compare the allotropes of carbon, rank intermolecular forces to explain physical properties, and at HL use sigma/pi bonds, hybridization and resonance.

keyterms.definition: A giant lattice of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout, e.g. diamond, graphite, SiO₂; very high melting point.
Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state, e.g. diamond, graphite, graphene, C₆₀.
Attractions between instantaneous and induced dipoles; present in all molecules and increase with number of electrons.
Attractions between permanent dipoles of polar molecules.
Strong dipole attraction between H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule.
Attractions between molecules (London, dipole–dipole, dipole–induced dipole, hydrogen bonding); much weaker than covalent bonds.
How much solute dissolves; "like dissolves like": polar solutes in polar solvents, non-polar in non-polar.
Distance moved by a component ÷ distance moved by the solvent front in chromatography.
Bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals, with electron density along the bond axis.
Bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below the bond axis.
Mixing of atomic orbitals to form new equivalent hybrid orbitals (sp, sp², sp³).
Two or more Lewis formulas for one species differing only in electron positions; the real structure is a hybrid.
Electrons shared by more than two atoms, spreading over several bonds, as in benzene and carbonate.

questions.prompt: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
options: Each C in graphite has one delocalized electron
questions.explanation: In graphite each C bonds to three others; the fourth electron is delocalized across the layer.

questions.statement: Diamond has a very high melting point because of strong covalent bonds throughout the structure.
questions.explanation: Melting requires breaking many strong C–C covalent bonds in the giant network.

questions.prompt: Match each allotrope to its structure.

pairs.right: Each C bonded to 4 others, tetrahedral
Layers of hexagons, weak forces between
A single layer of hexagonal carbon

questions.explanation: Same element, different bonding arrangements and properties.

questions.text: Silicon dioxide (quartz) has a covalent ___ structure.
questions.explanation: Each Si bonds to four O and each O to two Si in a giant 3D lattice.

questions.prompt: Why is graphite soft and useful as a lubricant?
options: Layers are held by weak London forces and slide
questions.explanation: Within layers bonds are strong; between layers only weak forces act.

questions.statement: Fullerene C₆₀ has a higher melting point than diamond.
questions.explanation: C₆₀ is molecular: only weak intermolecular forces hold the molecules together, so it sublimes at a much lower temperature.

questions.prompt: In diamond, the C–C–C bond angle is…
questions.explanation: Each carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to four others.

questions.text: Different forms of the same element are called ___.
questions.explanation: Allotropes differ in how atoms are bonded; isotopes differ in neutron number.

questions.prompt: Order these by melting point, lowest first.
questions.explanation: Iodine is molecular (weak London forces); NaCl is an ionic lattice; SiO₂ and diamond are covalent networks, with diamond highest.

questions.prompt: Which substance is a good conductor of electricity along its plane and is one atom thick?
questions.explanation: Graphene is a single graphite layer with delocalized electrons; it is very strong and conductive.

questions.prompt: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
questions.explanation: Methanol has an O–H group: H bonded to O can attract a lone pair on another O.

questions.statement: London forces exist between all molecules, polar or non-polar.
questions.explanation: Temporary dipoles arise in any electron cloud.

questions.prompt: Why does the boiling point of the halogens increase down group 17?
options: More electrons give stronger London forces
questions.explanation: Larger molecules with more electrons are more polarizable, so London forces are stronger.

questions.text: Water boils much higher than H₂S because of ___ bonding between water molecules.
questions.explanation: O is very electronegative and small, so O–H…O hydrogen bonds form; S–H bonds do not hydrogen bond significantly.

questions.prompt: Match each substance to its strongest intermolecular force.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding needs H on N, O or F; polar molecules have dipole–dipole forces.

questions.statement: When ethanol boils, its covalent C–O bonds are broken.
questions.explanation: Boiling a molecular substance overcomes intermolecular forces only; the molecules stay intact.

questions.prompt: Which is most soluble in hexane?
questions.explanation: Like dissolves like: non-polar I₂ dissolves in non-polar hexane via London forces.

questions.prompt: Order by boiling point, lowest first (all have similar molar masses).
questions.explanation: Similar London forces; propanal adds dipole–dipole forces; propanol adds hydrogen bonding.

questions.text: In chromatography, a spot travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 6.0 cm. Its Rf is ___.
questions.explanation: Rf = 3.0 / 6.0 = 0.50. Rf values are always between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: In paper chromatography with a non-polar solvent, which component will have the lowest Rf?
questions.explanation: Polar components are attracted to the polar stationary phase (water in the paper) and move least.

questions.prompt: How many σ and π bonds are in ethyne, H–C≡C–H?
questions.explanation: Every bond has one σ; the triple bond adds two π. Two C–H σ + one C–C σ = 3 σ.

questions.statement: A π bond is formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals.
questions.explanation: Electron density lies above and below the internuclear axis.

questions.prompt: Match each carbon to its hybridization.
questions.explanation: Count electron domains: 4 → sp³, 3 → sp², 2 → sp.

questions.text: The bond angle around an sp² hybridized carbon is about ___°.
questions.explanation: Three hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a triangle.

questions.prompt: In benzene, all C–C bonds are the same length because…
options: π electrons are delocalized over the ring
questions.explanation: The six π electrons are spread over all six carbons, giving bonds intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5).

questions.statement: Benzene readily undergoes addition reactions like alkenes.
questions.explanation: Addition would destroy the stable delocalized ring; benzene prefers substitution.

questions.prompt: What is the C–O bond order in the carbonate ion?
questions.explanation: Three resonance structures share one double bond across three C–O bonds: 4 bonding pairs / 3 bonds = 1.33.

questions.text: A π bond is ___ than a σ bond between the same atoms.
questions.explanation: Sideways overlap is less effective than head-on overlap, so π bonds are weaker and more reactive.
NO₃⁻ can be drawn with the N=O double bond in three equivalent positions.

questions.prompt: Order by C–C bond length, shortest first.
questions.explanation: Bond orders 3, 2, 1.5 and 1: higher bond order gives shorter bonds.
